meta.title: An AI agent coding skeptic tries AI agent coding, in excessive detail
meta.author: facundoolano

comments.author: briankung
comments.text:
Minor, but:


Historically, LLMs have been poor at generating Rust code due to its nicheness relative to Python and JavaScript.


I’ve never encountered this issue before. Almost every model that I’ve used has one shotted the Rust code I’ve wanted since very early on in LLM history.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text: [meta] It's quite entertaining to see these exchanges, and I suspect one of the factors that drives some "trad" developers up the wall (including the fierce faction here on Lobsters), is that the quality of LLM output is contextual. Even with model version, random seed being equal there are ~infinite factors (user prompt, harness prompt, repo context etc.) that influence output quality

comments.author: MrFantastik
comments.text: yea not to mention if the existing patterns in your code are garbage, the llms/agents will copy those garbage patterns w/o question. Likewise if patterns are good they will also be copied. This adds a sort of semantic gravity to your work and in my experience its a contributing factor to output quality

comments.author: tonyfinn
comments.text:
Most of my attempts at using LLMs with Rust with e.g. Claude 4 were with a project that used the Axum framework. It had serious difficulties producing a handler signature that would compile. Agentic tools sort of paper over this as it lets it loop over experimenting with the errors and shapes and go back for more information but that still a slow process. 4 also had similar difficulties with Kotlin that 4.5 resolved, so I'd guess 4.5 is better at Rust.

If you're talking like copilot or "manually pick the files for the context" iterations of tools (you know, mid 2025 tooling)? Not a hope.

comments.text: I also don’t know where this comes from. My experiments with Rust and Agentic Coding have always been extremely successful. At least for me.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: I do remember that last year (probably Claude 4 era) it seemed to have a hard time with the borrow checker (much as I did as a very experienced programmer but Rust beginner): being unable to give an actionable response to borrow checker errors or even consistently explain what they meant, and as a result going in circles trying to fix them, throwing in random lifetimes when the problem was the code was just not structured in a way that would ever work in Rust. With 4.5 and up, this hardly ever happens anymore.

comments.author: kana
comments.text:
So, I took a bit of time to install the mentioned nndex (v0.2.1) and run its benchmarks:

rows             1000   1000     10000   10000    50000    100000
dims             48     768      48      768      128      2
numpy_cpu        16717  30237    41739   870432   547596   213284
binding_cpu      9057   1092193  162588  951897   1809416  117342
ratio            1.85   0.03     0.26    0.91     0.30     1.82
---others---
binding_cpu_apx  6277   80657    9608    56702    75528    18300  # apx = ANN, different algorithm
binding_gpu      69586  194713   149784  2059208  1468505  258309
binding_gpu_apx  5846   51432    10329   77231    117768   30703


And the result doesn't look as good as the author claims. What's going wrong here? It turns out that the repo has two separate benchmarks, one under python_benchmarks/ that I run, and one used by the author in the blog post, under notebooks/. And it's the latter one that produced the wrong results: it asks numpy to normalize the whole matrix every time, while nndex does it only once at the beginning, and this made numpy run slower.

I don't doubt that the author (or Claude? who knows) can write correct benchmarks, as is showcased in python_benchmarks/, but I increasingly feel that vibecoding brings a trust problem. Even if the author has lots of open source contributions and seems proficient in Python, can I trust their vibecoded project? Can I trust their human-authored blog post presenting vibecoded benchmarks? Can I trust their README claiming huge performance boost? I don't know. I don't know.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
That doesn't seem specific to vibe coded stuff. Benchmarks and statistics are hard. People always made mistakes in them and you can find a tonne of similar examples. The language shootout was full of similar issues for years even though it's one of the most famous benchmarks.

In other words I think "Can I trust their human-authored blog post presenting vibecoded benchmarks?" can be reduced to "Can I trust (a) blog post presenting benchmarks?" - and the answer is the same as in 2023.

comments.author: twotwotwo
comments.text:
FWIW I think the distinction is beween a) 'skepticism' in the sense of, at a particular moment, doubting some particular claim or use and as b) skepticism as shorthand for being part of the community that is broadly, enduringly against LLMs and other recent generative stuff.

I'm not saying his definition of the word is the one right one; people do often use 'skepticism' just to broadly indicate what side someone is on. I'm saying these are both common uses of the word and he's got one use in mind while other people are thinking of the other one.

Since 2020 he'd been playing with this stuff. In the post you quote he decided he was no longer so doubtful that detailed instructions would make a difference because he'd seen more prompt adherence from newer iterations of the tech. (That doesn't mean he thought they could do, say, the things he does with them in this post; I can tell you they couldn't.) Later that year, after saying that, he said "Vibe coding with coding agents like Claude Code or Cursor is something I have little desire to even experiment with." Then later, after more specific changes named in the post, he said now he does find those tools interesting.

The effort to figure out how far the tech could go since 2020 could disqualify him "a skeptic" in the sense of being a part of the skeptical community. Disbelief in specific claims about the usefulness of specific tools or techniques at specific points in time also explains saying "I was skeptical that all this work on prompts mattered" or "I was skeptical of the utility of Claude Code/Codex." It is not surprising to me his opinion of the techs' capabilities changed as new things came out; the capabilities of lots of technologies do change over time.

Of course, understanding the definitions people are using doesn't bring people any closer together on the substance, and some folks will probably say that the post's usage is in some way illegitimate. But descriptively I think that's what is going on!
